claim: Notch pathway haploinsufficiency can cause severe developmental syndromes with highly variable penetrance.
source: Notch pathway haploinsufficiency can cause severe developmental syndromes with highly variable penetrance.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract about Notch haploinsufficiency that is supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Inserting an enhancer containing pioneer transcription factor sites coupled to Notch dimer sites can induce a subset of Notch haploinsufficiency phenotypes in Drosophila with wild type Notch gene dose.
source: Here, we unexpectedly found that inserting an enhancer containing pioneer transcription factor sites coupled to Notch dimer sites can induce a subset of Notch haploinsufficiency phenotypes in Drosophila with wild type Notch gene dose.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The enhancer induces Notch phenotypes in a Cdk8-dependent, transcription-independent manner.
source: Using Drosophila genetics, we show that this enhancer induces Notch phenotypes in a Cdk8-dependent, transcription-independent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic experiments and cell culture data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Changes in Notch signal production versus degradation differentially impact cellular outcomes that require long versus short signal duration.
source: We further combined mathematical modeling with quantitative trait and expression analysis to build a model that describes how changes in Notch signal production versus degradation differentially impact cellular outcomes that require long versus short signal duration.
evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical modeling combined with quantitative experimental data.

claim: Enhancers with specific binding sites promote rapid Cdk8-dependent Notch turnover via a 'bind and discard' mechanism.
source: Altogether, these findings support a 'bind and discard' mechanism in which enhancers with specific binding sites promote rapid Cdk8-dependent Notch turnover, and thereby reduce Notch-dependent transcription at other loci and sensitize tissues to gene dose based upon signal duration.
evidence: This is the main mechanistic conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental and modeling evidence.

claim: Notch haploinsufficiency was discovered in Drosophila.
source: For example, Notch (N) haploinsufficiency, which was discovered in Drosophila, causes a variety of tissue-specific defects including wing notching and extra sensory bristle formation that can vary greatly in penetrance and expressivity (Mohr, 1919).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citation to Mohr, 1919.

claim: Notch haploinsufficiency causes wing notching and extra sensory bristle formation in Drosophila.
source: For example, Notch (N) haploinsufficiency, which was discovered in Drosophila, causes a variety of tissue-specific defects including wing notching and extra sensory bristle formation that can vary greatly in penetrance and expressivity (Mohr, 1919).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Mohr, 1919).

claim: Notch1 heterozygous mice have heart valve and endothelium defects.
source: Notch pathway haploinsufficiency was subsequently observed in mammals, as Notch1 heterozygous mice have heart valve and endothelium defects (Nigam and Srivastava, 2009), whereas Notch2 heterozygotes have defects in bone, kidney and marginal zone B cells (Isidor et al., 2011; Simpson et al., 2011; Witt et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nigam and Srivastava, 2009.

claim: Notch2 heterozygous mice have defects in bone, kidney and marginal zone B cells.
source: Notch pathway haploinsufficiency was subsequently observed in mammals, as Notch1 heterozygous mice have heart valve and endothelium defects (Nigam and Srivastava, 2009), whereas Notch2 heterozygotes have defects in bone, kidney and marginal zone B cells (Isidor et al., 2011; Simpson et al., 2011; Witt et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Isidor et al., 2011; Simpson et al., 2011; Witt et al., 2003.

claim: Heterozygosity of NOTCH2 or JAG1 can cause Alagille syndrome in humans.
source: A single allele of NOTCH2 or the JAG1 ligand can also cause pathological phenotypes in humans, as heterozygosity of either gene can result in a variably penetrant developmental syndrome known as Alagille (McDaniell et al., 2006; Li et al., 1997; Oda et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to McDaniell et al., 2006; Li et al., 1997; Oda et al., 1997.

claim: Notch signaling is initiated by ligand-induced proteolysis of the Notch receptor to release NICD from the membrane.
source: Molecularly, Notch signaling is initiated by ligand-induced proteolysis of the Notch receptor to release the Notch intracellular domain (NICD) from the membrane (Kovall et al., 2017; Bray, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Notch signaling supported by citations.

claim: NICD transits into the nucleus and binds to CSL transcription factor and Mastermind to induce gene expression.
source: NICD subsequently transits into the nucleus, binds to the Cbf1/Su(H)/Lag1 (CSL) transcription factor (TF) and the adaptor protein Mastermind (Mam), and induces gene expression via two types of DNA binding sites: independent CSL sites that bind monomeric NICD/CSL/Mam (NCM) complexes, and Su(H) paired sites (SPS) that are oriented in a head-to-head manner to promote cooperative binding between two NCM complexes (Kovall et al., 2017; Bray, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Notch signaling mechanism supported by citations.

claim: Su(H) paired sites (SPS) are oriented in a head-to-head manner to promote cooperative binding between two NCM complexes.
source: NICD subsequently transits into the nucleus, binds to the Cbf1/Su(H)/Lag1 (CSL) transcription factor (TF) and the adaptor protein Mastermind (Mam), and induces gene expression via two types of DNA binding sites: independent CSL sites that bind monomeric NICD/CSL/Mam (NCM) complexes, and Su(H) paired sites (SPS) that are oriented in a head-to-head manner to promote cooperative binding between two NCM complexes (Kovall et al., 2017; Bray, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The NCM complex activates transcription via the P300 co-activator.
source: Once bound to an enhancer, the NCM complex activates transcription of associated genes via the P300 co-activator.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Notch transcriptional activation.

claim: Notch1 mutations that remove an NICD degron sequence are associated with increased NICD levels and T-ALL development.
source: In the mammalian blood system, for example, Notch1 mutations that remove an NICD degron sequence have been associated with increased NICD levels and the development of T-cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (T-ALL) in mice and humans (O'Neil et al., 2006; Weng et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to O'Neil et al., 2006; Weng et al., 2004.

claim: NICD turnover via the degron sequence is linked to transcription activation through Mam interaction with the Cdk8 kinase module.
source: Intriguingly, NICD turnover via this degron sequence has been directly linked to transcription activation, as the Mam protein interacts with the Cdk8 kinase module (CKM) of the Mediator complex, which can phosphorylate NICD to promote its ubiquitylation by the Fbxw7 E3-ligase and degradation by the proteasome (Fryer et al., 2004; Fryer et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fryer et al., 2004; Fryer et al., 2002.

claim: Gene mutations that lower CKM activity are associated with increased NICD levels and T-ALL.
source: Accordingly, gene mutations that lower CKM activity have also been associated with increased NICD levels and T-ALL initiation and progression (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Li et al., 2014.

claim: Both mouse and fly NCM proteins cooperatively bind the 1xSPS probe but not the 2xCSL probe.
source: In the absence of co-activators, RBPJ and Su(H) bound each probe additively with both the mouse and fly proteins showing a slightly higher affinity to 2xCSL than 1xSPS (note, the increased unbound 1xSPS probe (green) in lane 4 of Figure 1B and lane 3 of Figure 1C relative to unbound 2xCSL probe (magenta)). Including the NICD/Mam co-activators didn't change the additive binding behavior of RBPJ and Su(H) to 2xCSL. By contrast, both the mouse and fly NCM complex preferentially filled both sites of the 1xSPS probe relative to 2xCSL (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Flies homozygous for 6xSPS-3xGBE-lacZ (6SG-lacZ) develop a notched-wing phenotype that mimics Notch haploinsufficiency.
source: Surprisingly, flies homozygous for 6xSPS-3xGBE-lacZ (6SG-lacZ) developed a notched-wing phenotype that mimics a classic Notch haploinsufficiency (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Flies homozygous for 3xGBE alone, 6xSPS alone, or mutated SPSs do not develop wing notching phenotypes.
source: In contrast, flies homozygous for 3xGBE alone (G-lacZ), 6xSPS alone (6S-lacZ), or mutated SPSs (6SmutG-lacZ) (Tun et al., 1994) inserted in the same locus were indistinguishable from wild type (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: Flies with an equal number of Notch monomer (CSL) sites next to 3xGBE do not develop notched wings.
source: iii) Flies with an equal number of Notch monomer (CSL) sites next to 3xGBE did not develop notched wings (Figure 1J and L).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 1J and L.

claim: A single 6SG-lacZ transgene greatly enhances the penetrance and severity of wing notching in Notch heterozygotes.
source: We found that a single 6SG-lacZ transgene greatly enhanced the penetrance and severity of wing notching in N heterozygotes compared to either genotype alone (Figure 2A–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 2A–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Adding two extra alleles of Notch or removing one allele of Hairless significantly suppresses the notched wing phenotype induced by two copies of 6SG-lacZ.
source: Moreover, adding two extra alleles of N (4N) or removing one allele of H significantly suppressed the notched wing phenotype induced by two copies of 6SG-lacZ (Figure 2D–H).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 2D–H.

claim: 6SG-lacZ does not significantly impact macrochaetae formation in wild type or sensitized Notch and Hairless heterozygous backgrounds.
source: Intriguingly, 6SG-lacZ did not significantly impact macrochaetae formation in either wild type or sensitized N+/- and H+/- backgrounds (Figure 2J–L).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 2J–L.

claim: Two copies of 6SG-lacZ, but not 12CG-lacZ, significantly suppress the loss of L5 wing vein observed in Hairless heterozygotes.
source: However, while flies carrying two copies of the 6SG-lacZ Notch-dimer reporter alone did not cause a noticeable wing vein phenotype, two copies of the 6SG-lacZ, but not the 12CG-lacZ Notch-monomer reporter, did significantly suppress the loss of L5 wing vein observed in H+/- animals (Figure 2G–I).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 2G–I.

claim: Removing an allele of cdk8, cycC, kto, skd, or ago significantly suppresses the penetrance and severity of 6SG-induced wing nicking.
source: To do so, we removed an allele of each gene of the Cdk8-kinase module (CKM; cdk8 (Loncle et al., 2007), cycC (Loncle et al., 2007), kto (Med12) (Treisman, 2001), or skd (Med13) [Treisman, 2001]) or an allele of an E3-ligase that encodes the Drosophila homologue of Fbxw7 (archipelago, ago) [Moberg et al., 2001]) and found that each significantly suppressed the penetrance and severity of 6SG-induced wing nicking (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by genetic data in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Removing an allele of cycC, kto, skd or ago, but not cdk8, significantly suppresses wing notching in Notch heterozygotes.
source: Notably, we observed that in N heterozygotes, removing an allele of cycC, kto, skd or ago, but not cdk8, also significantly suppressed wing notching (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by genetic data in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The wing notching penetrance and severity is similar with promoter-containing and promoter-less transgenes.
source: We found that the wing notching penetrance and severity was similar with both transgenes, and the wing phenotype generated by both was significantly suppressed by removing an allele of skd (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 3D.

claim: A transcriptionally active promoter is not required to induce wing nicks.
source: These findings suggest that a transcriptionally active promoter is not required to induce wing nicks.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing similar phenotypes with and without promoters.

claim: Actinomycin-D effectively inhibits Notch-induced transcription but does not alter N1ICD half-life or mobility.
source: Importantly, we found that while actinomycin-D effectively inhibited Notch-induced transcription (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), it neither altered N1ICD half-life in the split-luciferase assay (Figure 3E), nor altered N1ICD mobility in western blot analysis (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 3E, 3F, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Inhibiting Cdk8 activity using Senexin-A or SEL120-34A significantly prolongs N1ICD half-life.
source: In contrast, inhibiting Cdk8 activity using Senexin-A or SEL120-34A, two structurally distinct and specific inhibitors of Cdk8 and Cdk19, a closely related vertebrate paralogue that is absent in Drosophila (Porter et al., 2012; Rzymski et al., 2017), significantly prolonged N1ICD half-life in the split-luciferase assay (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: N1ICD is stabilized in mammalian cells deficient for RBPJ, MAML proteins, or treated with SEL120-34A.
source: Importantly, we found that N1ICD was stabilized in mammalian OT11 cells deficient for RBPJ (Figure 3H; Kato et al., 1997), in mK4 cells deficient for the three Mastermind-like (MAML) proteins, and in mK4 cells treated with SEL120-34A (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–E.

claim: Cdk8-mediated regulation of NICD degradation requires NCM complex formation on DNA but does not require active transcription.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that Cdk8-mediated regulation of NICD degradation requires NCM complex formation on DNA in both mammalian cells and fly tissues but does not require active transcription.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experimental findings from cell culture and genetic studies.

claim: GFP levels decrease as a function of added GBE-SPS sites in wing margin cells.
source: We found that GFP levels decreased as a function of added GBE-SPS sites (Figure 4D–H).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by quantitative imaging data in Figure 4D–H.

claim: The ratio between slopes of GFP expression in wild type and skd heterozygotes is 1.88 ± 0.29, in agreement with the predicted 2-fold change.
source: The ratio between slopes as calculated by linear regression analysis of GFP levels in wild type and skd heterozygotes (solid lines in Figure 4A) was 1.88 ± 0.29, in agreement with the predicted 2-fold change in the absence of CKM dosage compensation.
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of experimental data that matches model predictions.

claim: Removing an allele of each CKM gene does not significantly suppress the Notch haploinsufficiency of extra macrochaetae.
source: In contrast to the observed suppression of wing notching (Figure 3B), we found that removing an allele of each CKM gene did not significantly suppress the Notch haploinsufficiency of extra macrochaetae (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 4J.

claim: Macrochaetae numbers further increase in Notch;cdk8 and Notch;skd compound heterozygotes.
source: In fact, macrochaetae numbers further increased in N;cdk8 and N;skd compound heterozygotes, which is opposite of the predicted outcome if slowing NICD degradation significantly elevated NICD levels during macrochaetae formation (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 4J.

claim: Maintenance of wing margin identity is a continuous process at least 48 hours long.
source: Maintenance of wing margin identity is a continuous process at least 48 hours long (de Celis et al., 1996; Shellenbarger and Mohler, 1978), whereas macrochaetae formation requires Notch input over a short time period (< 30 min) (Barad et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to de Celis et al., 1996; Shellenbarger and Mohler, 1978.

claim: Macrochaetae formation requires Notch input over a short time period (< 30 min).
source: Maintenance of wing margin identity is a continuous process at least 48 hours long (de Celis et al., 1996; Shellenbarger and Mohler, 1978), whereas macrochaetae formation requires Notch input over a short time period (< 30 min) (Barad et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Barad et al., 2010.

claim: Flies carrying two copies of G6Ssyn-lacZ versus G6Sm8-lacZ show highly similar penetrance and severity of wing notching phenotypes.
source: Comparative analysis of flies carrying two copies of the synthetic G6S(syn)-lacZ versus the G6Sm8-lacZ revealed a highly similar penetrance and severity of wing notching phenotypes (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 5B.

claim: An endogenous SPS sequence from E(spl)m8 can promote NICD degradation to induce wing notching in the GBE-SPS transgene assay.
source: Thus, an endogenous SPS sequence from a known Notch-regulated enhancer can promote NICD degradation to induce a wing notching phenotype in the GBE-SPS transgene assay, even in the presence of potential negative feedback.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental comparison of synthetic and endogenous SPS sequences.

claim: Flies containing two copies of 5xZld-6xSPS-lacZ induce notched wings, whereas flies with 5xZld-lacZ or 5xZld-12xCSL-lacZ do not.
source: Accordingly, we found that flies containing two copies of 5xZld-6xSPS-lacZ induced notched wings, whereas flies with 5xZld-lacZ or 5xZld-12xCSL-lacZ failed to induce wing notching (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 5C.

claim: 5xEbox sites fail to induce wing phenotypes when coupled to either SPS or CSL sites.
source: In contrast, 5xEbox sites failed to induce wing phenotypes when coupled to either SPS or CSL sites (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 5D.

claim: Pioneer TFs synergize with SPS Notch dimer sites, but not CSL Notch monomer sites, to promote Notch degradation.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that TFs with pioneering activity synergize with the SPS Notch dimer sites, but not the CSL Notch monomer sites, to promote Notch degradation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential effects of pioneer TFs with SPS versus CSL sites.

claim: Notch heterozygous flies carrying a single copy of 6S-lacZ have significantly enhanced wing notching compared to Notch heterozygous flies with 0S-lacZ.
source: Importantly, we found that Notch heterozygous flies carrying a single copy of the 6S-lacZ transgene had significantly enhanced wing notching compared to Notch heterozygous flies with an enhancer-less lacZ transgene (0S-lacZ) (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 5E.

claim: Enhancers with only SPS sites can promote NICD degradation, but to a lesser degree than those near a bound pioneer TF.
source: Taken together with the finding that G6S-lacZ and 5xZld-6S-lacZ were sufficient to induce notched wings in wild type flies (Figure 1K and Figure 5C) whereas 6S-lacZ failed to do so (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), these data suggest that enhancers with only SPS sites can promote NICD degradation, but to a lesser degree than those near a bound pioneer TF.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparing phenotypes of different transgene constructs.

claim: The 'bind and discard' mechanism reveals an unexpected global link between accessible binding sites in the epigenome.
source: This 'bind and discard' mechanism reveals an unexpected global link between accessible binding sites in the epigenome, such that the collective 'drain' loci can reduce Notch-dependent transcription at other loci in the same nucleus.
evidence: This is a conceptual conclusion based on the experimental findings and modeling.

claim: Seemingly non-functional genomic binding events could impact TF metabolism in a Cdk8-dependent manner.
source: Moreover, since the binding sites do not have to be coupled with transcription to induce a notched wing phenotype, our findings highlight the possibility that seemingly non-functional genomic binding events could impact TF metabolism in a Cdk8-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the finding that transcription is not required for the phenotype.

claim: About one third of direct Notch target genes in human T-ALL are regulated by SPS sites.
source: Recent studies found that about one third of direct Notch target genes (38 of 107 genes) in human T-ALL are regulated by SPS sites (Severson et al., 2017), and a mouse mK4 cell line has an estimated 2500 Notch dimer dependent binding sites (Hass et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Severson et al., 2017 and Hass et al., 2015.

claim: A mouse mK4 cell line has an estimated 2500 Notch dimer dependent binding sites.
source: Recent studies found that about one third of direct Notch target genes (38 of 107 genes) in human T-ALL are regulated by SPS sites (Severson et al., 2017), and a mouse mK4 cell line has an estimated 2500 Notch dimer dependent binding sites (Hass et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hass et al., 2015.

claim: Eight of 154 Notch-responsive genes in a Drosophila wing disc-derived cell line encode E(spl) genes clustered within a common 40 kb locus.
source: However, of the 154 Notch-responsive genes identified in a Drosophila wing disc-derived cell line, eight encode E(spl) genes that are clustered within a common 40 kb locus and many E(spl) genes contain one or more SPS sites (Housden et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Housden et al., 2013.

claim: Notch1 mutations that remove the NICD PEST domain are common in T-ALL.
source: For example, mutations in the NICD PEST domain that decouple DNA binding and degradation are common in T-ALL (Weng et al., 2004), and CycC (CCNC) functions as a haploinsufficient tumor suppressor gene in T-ALL, at least in part, by stabilizing NICD (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Weng et al., 2004.

claim: CycC (CCNC) functions as a haploinsufficient tumor suppressor gene in T-ALL by stabilizing NICD.
source: For example, mutations in the NICD PEST domain that decouple DNA binding and degradation are common in T-ALL (Weng et al., 2004), and CycC (CCNC) functions as a haploinsufficient tumor suppressor gene in T-ALL, at least in part, by stabilizing NICD (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Li et al., 2014.

claim: T-ALL cells are 'addicted' to Notch and dependent on a long duration signal.
source: These findings suggest that T-ALL is highly sensitive to alterations in NICD degradation. Indeed, T-ALL cells are 'addicted' to Notch and are thus dependent on a long duration signal (Severson et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Severson et al., 2017.

claim: About 30% of Notch target genes in T-ALL use SPS containing enhancers.
source: As ~30% of Notch target genes in T-ALL use SPS containing enhancers, our findings provide insight into how Notch PEST truncations and CCNC heterozygotes could each promote tumorigenesis by slowing CKM-mediated NICD turnover on SPS enhancers.
evidence: This is a statement based on prior studies and the current findings.
